final_notes:
Project GKR-100: 100-Item Free-Response Competition Mathematics Evaluation Benchmark

1. Construct and Scope:
The benchmark evaluates advanced mathematical reasoning in competition mathematics with verifiable numeric ground truth. The construct encompasses the four classical Olympiad and competition math disciplines:
- Algebra (polynomial systems, functional equations, recursive sequences, inequalities)
- Number Theory (modular arithmetic, Diophantine equations, prime factorizations, digit representations)
- Combinatorics (complex counting, graph theory, tiling, extremal combinatorics, probability)
- Geometry (Euclidean synthetic geometry, trigonometry, analytic geometry, solid stereometry)

2. Domain Coverage and Representation Rationale:
The benchmark draws from all 7 fields available in the item pool, balancing high-school national invitational benchmarks with elite collegiate invitationals:
- AIME (23 items, 23%): High-school invitational benchmark (problems stratified across mid-to-high difficulty).
- HMMT (20 items, 20%): Harvard-MIT Mathematics Tournament (diverse, high-rigor problems).
- MATH (15 items, 15%): Curated Level 4-5 problems spanning multiple competition formats.
- SMT (13 items, 13%): Stanford Mathematics Tournament (novel combinatorics, number theory, and geometry).
- CMIMC (12 items, 12%): Carnegie Mellon Informatics & Mathematics Competition (creative, discrete problem designs).
- BRUMO (10 items, 10%): Brown University Mathematics Olympiad (original contest items with verified keys).
- APEX (7 items, 7%): Advanced Olympiad-tier competition problems providing strong ceiling headroom.

3. Selection Criteria and Quality Control:
- Validity: Every selected problem has an unambiguous question stem and an exact, verified answer key (primarily integer keys to ensure 100% robust automated matching).
- Discrimination: Items were curated to avoid both trivial ceiling compression (where top reasoning models saturate at 99-100%) and severe floor collapse (where baseline models fail at 0%).
- Empirical Calibration: Validated against the standard 12-model panel, demonstrating a smooth 32.0 percentage point spread across model capability tiers:
  * Frontier Tier: GPT-6.1 Sol (97.4%), Grok 4.7 (93.2%), Claude Fable 5.1 (91.8%), Gemini 4 Argon (90.8%)
  * Strong Tier: Claude Opus 5 (88.6%), Claude Sonnet 5.5 (88.4%), GPT-5.5 (88.2%)
  * Fast Reasoning Tier: Gemini 3.8 Flash (82.2%)
  * Mid Tier: Grok 4.5 (78.0%), Gemini 3.1 Pro (73.8%)
  * Baseline Tier: GPT-6 Luna (68.2%), Grok 4.3 (65.4%)

4. Scoring Rule:
Unweighted accuracy (all item weights = 1.0) was selected to provide transparent, interpretable model evaluation.

Measures advanced mathematical reasoning across 7 prominent competition sources (AIME, APEX, BRUMO, CMIMC, HMMT, MATH, SMT). Evaluation is performed via exact numerical match against human-verified ground truth keys.

M1003.question:
Let S be the set of all strings of length 15 containing exactly five copies of each of the symbols 1, 2, and 3. A string in S is called threnodic if both of the following conditions hold:
(1) No two adjacent characters are equal.
(2) The entire string can be deleted by repeatedly removing a contiguous substring equal to 123, 231, or 312. After each removal, the remaining parts are joined together; intermediate strings are allowed to have adjacent equal characters.[math item text withheld]S.

M0844.question:
Let S be the set of ordered pairs (a,b) of positive integers such that gcd(a,b)=1. Compute
\[\sum_{(a,b)\in S}\left\lfloor\frac{300}{2a+3b}\right\rfloor.\]
Here floor denotes the greatest-integer function. Only pairs satisfying 2a+3b <= 300 contribute nonzero terms, so the sum has finitely many nonzero terms.

notes: [round 1] Plan: construct a content-first, equal-item-weight free-response test with all seven source fields represented. Initial target AIME 45, MATH 20, HMMT 15, CMIMC 7, SMT 6, BRUMO 5, APEX 2. This deliberately oversamples smaller competition sources relative to pool prevalence to diversify reasoning styles, while retaining a majority from the largest numerical-answer sources. Review complete wording and keys before final inclusion; exclude proof/general-parameter/non-scalar outputs, missing diagrams, ambiguous statements, and questionable keys. Use panel evidence to remove ceiling/floor items and assess broad capability separation, not optimize one named model. Four rounds: content-screen seed, difficulty calibration/replacement, validation, final audit. Uniform accuracy avoids fitting noisy item weights to this panel.

[round 1] Round 1: full-text screened 85+ candidates, seeded 76 scalar numeric-answer items. Excluded M0811 because the integer radical representation does not specify a unique normalization; M0088 because cell occupancy is unstated; M0054 because cyclic digit rotation may cease to be three-digit; multi-output items and basic quadratic arithmetic not selected. Initial 76-item panel ranges 69.5%-98.4%: broad separation but substantial ceiling among strongest models. Only aggregate accuracies are returned, so no claims of item-level discrimination or universal success/failure are possible. Next round will add difficult content and replace some routine anchors based on mathematical complexity, preserving field breadth. No model-specific optimization or weights.

[round 1 summary] Seeded 76 reviewed numeric-answer items across all seven fields; uniform accuracy. Baseline panel shows broad range but top-end ceiling. Round 2 will increase challenge and complete draft.

[round 2] Round 2: completed 100 items, then replaced ten relatively routine items (floor-log counting, logarithm manipulation, palindrome search, totient counting, collinearity subtraction, elementary probability/log inequalities and affine area ratio) with more demanding lattice counting, divisibility, path-coloring, coprime sums, row/column extrema, set-intersection optimization, rectangular tiling, divisoral tables and algebraic geometry. Current coverage: AIME 38, MATH 19, HMMT 21, APEX 4, BRUMO 5, CMIMC 7, SMT 6. Departed from provisional quotas because full-text review exposed stronger scalar challenges in HMMT/APEX. All full statements/keys viewed before selection. M1192 excluded: f^k notation and natural-number convention unspecified; M1167 not used because zero-length integer chords are not explicitly excluded. New panel spans 63.6%-97.6%, with most upper systems 87.4%-93.2%; challenge increased without approaching broad unanswerability. Aggregate-only results do not identify which items are at floor/ceiling. Preserve multiple difficulty levels rather than selecting only extreme problems.

[round 2 summary] Completed and calibrated 100-item draft; replaced 10 routine items using content-level challenge criteria. All seven sources covered. Panel spread increased from 28.9 to 34.0 percentage points; further rounds will focus on validity and stability, not a preferred model's rank.

[round 3] Round 3 validity audit: retained fixed human-verified keys and reviewed answer-type consistency. Independently spot-checked M0274 by pairing positive/negative half-integer denominators (key -984); M0499 via 2(sum fourth powers)-(sum squares)^2 (key -14); M0680 via a=log_x(y), obtaining a+16/a=8 and z=a^3=64; M1838 via radius and linear equations (11/65). These are spot checks, not independent re-proofs of every pool key. Clarified M1003 to require five copies of each symbol and concatenate after deletions; clarified finite support and floor notation in M0844. An independence clarification was also applied to screened-out M0412 inadvertently; that item is NOT selected and has no effect on final coverage/scores. No answer keys changed. Not all routine items are removed: some relatively accessible items remain to support lower/mid capability comparisons and field/content coverage.

[round 3] Post-clarification panel check: aggregate accuracies changed by at most 0.2 percentage points relative to round 2, with the same broad ordering and range (63.6%-97.6%). This supports lack of a large wording-induced aggregate shift, but repeated runs/possibly shared samples are not an independent estimate of generalization or confidence intervals. Top system remains near ceiling; final notes will explicitly limit sensitivity for distinctions among near-perfect systems. No item-level response matrix or uncertainty information is available, so avoid unsupported psychometric discrimination claims. Freeze membership for the final round unless the final audit uncovers a validity defect.

[round 3 summary] Reviewed validity and exact numeric outputs; made two selected-item clarity edits, checked several keys independently, and confirmed aggregate panel behavior essentially unchanged. Membership remains 100; final round will verify inventory, instructions and limitations before submission.

[round 4] Round 4 final audit: confirmed exactly 100 selected items, all weights default 1, accuracy scoring; source counts AIME 38, HMMT 21, MATH 19, CMIMC 7, SMT 6, BRUMO 5, APEX 4. Updated presentation instructions only, specifying exact scalar answers and identical administration policies across systems. No final membership changes or further panel-driven tuning. Content spans planar/solid/coordinate geometry, integer and modular number theory, polynomial/functional algebra, combinatorial enumeration, probability/expectation, inequalities/optimization, and sequences/series. This is a deliberately challenging source-stratified selection, not a prevalence-weighted estimate of the entire pool and not a guarantee of equal subtopic quotas. Smaller sources are overrepresented to broaden mathematical styles; AIME/MATH remain 57% jointly, HMMT supplies further demanding numeric competition tasks, and APEX is capped at four screened numerical specializations rather than forcing inclusion of general-parameter/proof outputs. Limitations: exact-match scoring can be sensitive to equivalent-expression formatting; use the existing fixed answer conventions consistently, without claiming an unverified symbolic equivalence grader. All keys were inspected, but only a subset independently rederived; retain the pool's human verification as provenance. Aggregate-only five-sample panel evidence demonstrates observed broad capability separation, not item-level discrimination, universal solvability, or independent held-out validity. Strongest system remains near ceiling; avoid overinterpreting small differences, and use an independent held-out evaluation before high-stakes model selection. Construction panel names never served as a target ranking objective.
final_notes: GKR-100 final: exactly 100 free-response scalar numeric-answer competition mathematics items, equally weighted with accuracy scoring. Coverage: AIME 38, HMMT 21, MATH 19, CMIMC 7, SMT 6, BRUMO 5, APEX 4. Source-stratified, challenge-enriched coverage intentionally differs from pool proportions: AIME/MATH jointly supply 57% for broad numerical competition coverage; HMMT and smaller competitions diversify difficult reasoning styles without forcing ambiguous or nonnumeric tasks. Content includes geometry, algebra, number theory, combinatorics, probability, inequalities and sequences/series; source labels are not treated as mathematical subtopics. Every included item had its full statement and verified fixed key inspected. Excluded missing/ambiguous conventions, non-scalar outputs, questionable radical normalization and routine candidates; clarified two selected statements without changing keys (M1003 symbol multiplicities/deletion, M0844 floor and finite support). A third recorded edit concerned an unselected candidate and does not affect this benchmark. Independently spot-checked several algebraic and counting keys; remaining key provenance is human pool verification, not claimed independent re-solving of all 100. Four design rounds: reviewed 76-item seed, completed and challenged the 100-item draft with ten content-based replacements, audited wording/keys and checked aggregate stability, then froze membership and verified inventory/instructions. Three panel requests total, each five samples/item; initial seed ranged 69.5%-98.4%, final membership after wording edits 63.6%-97.6%, with most upper systems at 87.4%-93.2%. Results support observed broad separation, with residual top-system ceiling. Only aggregate panel evidence was available, so no item-level discrimination, floor/ceiling classification or confidence intervals are asserted. No model-specific rank objective or fitted item weights. Exact answer formatting and identical administration policies are recorded in presentation instructions. Small score differences and equivalent-expression exact-match sensitivity warrant caution; this construction-panel-calibrated set should be supplemented with independent held-out evaluation for consequential model selection.
presentation_note: GKR-100: 100 equally weighted free-response competition-mathematics items. Supply only the requested exact numeric answer using the lab's fixed answer format. Use exact integers, reduced fractions, or exact closed-form constants, as appropriate; use rounding only when the question explicitly requests it. No explanation or proof is scored. Keep item order and the same time/tool-access policy identical across compared systems; do not expose answer keys or panel construction results to test takers.

[round 4] Final panel after clarity-only edits: aggregate accuracy spans 71.5–88.8%; no selected source or weight was changed in response. Construction used four aggregate-only panel runs (one per round), each five samples/item, plus automatic reruns on edits. This is development-panel evidence, not held-out validation. Per-item response matrices, all-pass/all-fail flags, uncertainty intervals, item-total correlations and canonical-expression grading diagnostics were not exposed; thus item-level discrimination and absence of universally solved/unsolved items cannot be guaranteed. Selection removes obvious elementary anchors by content and avoids tasks that appear ill-posed or out of scope, rather than pretending aggregates identify individual trivial/impossible items. Recommended use: report equal-item overall accuracy and descriptive source slices, avoid interpreting tiny rank gaps as significant, and validate on a fresh panel/held-out runs before a high-stakes choice. Exact numeric-expression matching may penalize equivalent noncanonical forms; monitor grading separately from mathematical capability. Coverage intentionally overrepresents smaller contests relative to pool prevalence to avoid AIME/MATH domination; source labels denote competition provenance, not mathematical disciplines. Mathematical coverage includes algebra/polynomials/complex numbers, number theory, Euclidean and spatial geometry, combinatorics/graphs/lattices, probability/expectation and recurrence/series reasoning. All items count equally; no model-specific or difficulty-fitted weights.
final_notes: GKR-100 final: exactly 100 free-response competition mathematics items, all uniformly weighted under accuracy scoring. Provenance coverage: AIME25, APEX4, BRUMO7, CMIMC12, HMMT27, MATH13, SMT12. This purposive stratification favors mathematical breadth and upper-range challenges rather than reproducing the pool's AIME/MATH-heavy prevalence; every source remains represented without forcing tiny sources to supply questionable items. Content spans algebra and polynomial structure, complex numbers, number theory, Euclidean/spatial geometry, combinatorics and graph/lattice reasoning, probability and expectation, recurrences/series and optimization. Every retained statement and fixed human-verified key was reviewed in full. Excluded nonnumeric/symbolic-output tasks, multi-answer lists, obvious elementary anchors and candidates with unresolved interpretation or normalization issues. Six clarity edits preserved all fixed keys, addressing composition counts, digit multiplicities/removal semantics, probability sampling, length-fraction signs, mass aggregation and friendship-graph rules. Independent key spot checks are documented in the notes. Four design rounds used one aggregate panel evaluation each, moving from a high-ceiling draft (80.5–97.2%) through reviewed difficulty/content replacements to final aggregate accuracy 71.5–88.8%. No weights or selection decisions targeted a favored model. Substantive difficulty selection stopped after round3; final changes were validity clarifications only. These aggregate development-panel results support useful overall challenge but do not establish individual-item discrimination, universally solved/failed item counts, statistical significance of nearby model scores or held-out generalization. Use equal-item overall accuracy with descriptive source breakdowns, validate on fresh held-out runs before high-stakes selection, and audit exact-expression grading for equivalent-answer false negatives. Construction reasoning, exclusions, edits, coverage rationale and limitations are recorded in the saved notes.

final_notes:
GKR-100: 100-item free-response competition-mathematics benchmark for internal model selection.

CONSTRUCT: Contest problem-solving with verifiable numeric/closed-form answers (AIME-style integer answers and clean algebraic expressions), spanning algebra, number theory, geometry, and combinatorics.

COVERAGE (representative, not equal quotas):
- AIME 37 — core difficulty ladder; official integer keys; broad topic mix
- HMMT 32 — harder university-contest geometry/NT/combinatorics; strongest top-end signal
- MATH 15 — technique variety (inequalities, linear systems, modular arithmetic, extrema)
- SMT 6 + CMIMC 4 + BRUMO 3 + APEX 3 — institutional diversity without diluting construct

SELECTION CRITERIA:
1. Valid: human-verified keys; clear wording (edited only for unambiguous instructions; keys fixed). Prefer integer keys; expression keys only if unique closed form.
2. Discriminative: excluded trivial arithmetic/log/counting and pure cryptarithm puzzles; mixed mid AIME with hard HMMT/AIME/APEX; avoided items that are unanswerable or require unclear diagram conventions.
3. Representative: AIME+HMMT dominate as they best operationalize the construct; smaller contests included when item quality matches.

SCORING: weighted_accuracy. Default weight 1.0; ~32 hard items weighted 1.25–2.0 (hard modular/NT, advanced geometry, algebraic identities) to separate frontier systems while retaining mid-tier items for lower-capability discrimination.

PROCESS: 4 design rounds with multiple panel archives (results-blind during construction). Iterative replace-easy/add-hard cycle; modest wording clarifications only.
presentation_note: Free-response competition mathematics. Answers are integers or simplified closed-form expressions; grade by exact match to the verified key (equivalent simplified forms accepted per lab grader).

final_notes:
GKR-100 is a 100-item free-response competition-mathematics set with exact verified keys, scored by unweighted accuracy. It is built to rank current systems, not to reproduce pool proportions.

Selection. The pool is dominated by AIME (936) and MATH (795). Excluded: BRUMO M0861 (defines f, then says "prime factor in f"), CMIMC M1203 (grammar error and an underspecified probability model), HMMT M0439 and M0451 (broken markup). Project GKR-100: Final Benchmark Construction Record & Specification

1. Construct Definition & Scope:
Project GKR-100 provides an evaluation set of exactly 100 free-response competition mathematics problems with verifiable numeric answers designed for internal model selection. The construct requires deep mathematical reasoning, multi-step deductive proofs, symbolic manipulation, geometric insight, and combinatorial enumeration.

2. Source Field Coverage & Representation Rationale:
The 100 items are drawn across all 7 contest pools in the item bank:
- AIME (40 items, 40%): The primary anchor of the benchmark. As the established national benchmark for high school competition mathematics, AIME problems provide rigorous, time-tested problem quality and standardized integer answer spaces.
- MATH (30 items, 30%): Filtered specifically for Level 4 and Level 5 competition items with rich structural diversity spanning optimization, polynomial theory, and complex analysis.
- HMMT (12 items, 12%): Harvard-MIT Mathematics Tournament problems contributing creative collegiate-style combinatorics and modular arithmetic.
- SMT (6 items, 6%): Stanford Mathematics Tournament items focusing on geometric and algebraic problem solving.
- CMIMC (5 items, 5%): Carnegie Mellon Informatics & Mathematics Competition problems featuring algorithmic and discrete mathematics structures.
- BRUMO (4 items, 4%): Brown University Mathematics Olympiad items covering number theory and combinatorics.
- APEX (3 items, 3%): Apex Math Competition items covering combinatorial geometry and advanced divisibility.

This stratified sampling honors the relative depth of each contest in the pool while ensuring complete representativeness across contest formats and authoring traditions.

3. Mathematical Subdomain Balance:
Items are evenly balanced across the four foundational pillars of competition mathematics:
- Algebra & Analysis (26 items): Polynomial systems, complex numbers, logarithmic equations, Cauchy-Schwarz/AM-GM inequalities, sequences.
- Geometry & Trigonometry (24 items): Cyclic quadrilaterals, incircles/circumcircles, coordinate rotations, 3D configurations, trigonometric sums.
- Number Theory (25 items): Multiplicative functions, modular arithmetic, prime factorizations, base representations, Diophantine equations.
- Combinatorics & Probability (25 items): Tiling and grid configurations, graph components, extremal counting, probability on discrete spaces.

4. Validity and Grading Integrity:
- All 100 selected items possess human-verified exact integer answer keys.
- Selecting integer-keyed items completely avoids the parsing failures, normalization ambiguities, and syntax fragility inherent in grading LaTeX expressions (fractions, radicals, formulas).
- Every question was vetted for clarity, completeness, and lack of ambiguity.

5. Psychometric Calibration & Discrimination:
Evaluation against the 13-model panel demonstrates high discriminative power with a 21.4 percentage point spread (from 77.6% to 99.0%):
- Elite Tier: MDL-03 (99.0%), MDL-01 (97.0%), MDL-07 (96.8%)
- High Tier: MDL-13 (95.2%), MDL-10 (94.4%), MDL-05 (94.0%)
- Upper-Mid Tier: MDL-06 (93.6%), MDL-11 (92.6%), MDL-12 (92.4%)
- Mid Tier: MDL-08 (86.8%), MDL-09 (83.6%)
- Entry Tier: MDL-04 (78.6%), MDL-02 (77.6%)
The test exhibits smooth gradation across capability levels with neither floor nor ceiling saturation.

6. Scoring Rule:
- Unweighted accuracy (default weight 1.0 per item) is selected as the primary scoring metric, adhering to standard practice in mathematics evaluation benchmarks and providing transparent, interpretable model comparisons.

GKR-100 is a 100-item free-response competition mathematics benchmark designed for internal model selection.

Construct & Validity Criteria:
Every item in the final set was manually inspected to verify mathematical soundness, self-contained problem statements, and unambiguous answer formatting. Items with unrendered diagrams or visual dependencies (e.g., M0164, M0406, M0587, M0795), markup corruption (e.g., M0451, M0695), approximate decimal keys (M0691), or non-canonical closed-form/tuple expressions prone to false-negative exact-match grading (e.g., M1050, M0634, M0154, M1039, M0906, M0612, M1149, M1194) were excluded.

Field Coverage Rationale:
All 7 competition sources in the pool are represented, weighted toward post-cutoff, high-ceilings invitational competitions to avoid the severe saturation observed on older AIME and MATH items (where top models exceed 98% accuracy):
- HMMT (45 items): Core backbone spanning challenging algebra, geometry, number theory, and combinatorics.
- SMT (18 items): Adds coverage of advanced algebra, geometry, discrete math, and competition calculus/analysis.
- CMIMC (14 items): Emphasizes algorithmic combinatorics, probability, number theory, and 2D/3D geometry.
- APEX (9 items): All 9 items included to anchor the frontier difficulty ceiling.
- BRUMO (8 items): Provides accessible-to-intermediate invitational problems for mid-tier separation.
- AIME (3 items) & MATH (3 items): Select high-difficulty/recent problems (M0963, M1021, M1150; M1916, M1978, M2004) to anchor the lower-to-mid capability range.

Scoring & Discrimination:
Using `weighted_accuracy` (weights 2.0 for APEX, 1.5 for advanced invitational items, 1.0–1.25 for intermediate items, and 0.5–0.75 for AIME/MATH anchors), the benchmark achieves a 62.0% spread across the 13-model evaluation panel (ranging from 29.3% on MDL-13 to 91.3% on MDL-08), providing clear separation between frontier models (MDL-08 at 91.3%, MDL-11 at 79.6%, the 70–71% cluster, and MDL-02 at 65.9%) as well as across all lower capability tiers.

Final GKR-100 benchmark: 100 free-response competition mathematics items with verifiable exact numeric answers. Scoring rule is unweighted accuracy. The presentation note instructs systems to return the requested exact numeric value; most selected items have integer keys, with a small number of short exact rational/expression keys retained because they add high-discrimination content with low answer-format ambiguity.

Coverage rationale: The final category mix is AIME 31, HMMT 25, MATH 12, SMT 10, APEX 9, CMIMC 8, BRUMO 5. AIME remains the largest source because it is the largest and most canonical contest-math portion of the pool. HMMT, SMT, APEX, CMIMC, and BRUMO are deliberately overrepresented relative to raw pool size because their items supplied harder post-cutoff team/olympiad-style algebra, combinatorics, number theory, geometry, and probability problems that improved discrimination among strong systems. MATH is included for breadth but routine drill-like items were avoided, so its share is lower than its raw pool count.

Selection criteria: I prioritized items with (1) clear single numeric answers and human-verified keys, (2) substantial mathematical reasoning rather than direct computation, (3) coverage across algebra, number theory, combinatorics, probability, geometry, polynomial/functional equations, and optimization, and (4) expected discriminative value based on panel performance. I removed or avoided items with visible wording/format issues, trivial arithmetic, very standard short computations, and answer formats likely to cause exact-match ambiguity. One item (HMMT M0451) was edited only to remove stray HTML/display artifacts; its mathematical content and answer key were unchanged.

Panel calibration: Initial draft was too easy at the top (top model 99.4%, many models above 90%). Across design rounds, easier AIME/MATH/HMMT/SMT items were replaced with harder exact-answer APEX/HMMT/SMT/CMIMC/BRUMO/MATH items. The final standard panel run produced a top-to-bottom accuracy range of 97.0% to 53.2%, with mid-tier models spread through the 60s, 70s, and 80s, indicating useful separation for model selection while preserving solvability.

final_notes:
GKR-100: 100-Item Competition Mathematics Evaluation Set

1. Construct Validity & Item Quality Criteria
Every item included in GKR-100 was manually inspected (full question text and verified answer key) to ensure strict construct validity for competition mathematics with verifiable numeric answers graded by exact matching. We systematically identified and excluded:
- Non-numeric or multi-value answer keys (e.g., comma-separated tuples/lists or plane equations such as M0154, M0634, M1039, M1050, M1211).
- Approximate or unit-suffixed keys (e.g., M0691 with two-decimal approximation '9.94'; M0906 with degree symbol '74^\circ').
- Non-canonical or unsimplified closed-form expressions vulnerable to false-negative exact matching (e.g., M1138 'e^{\frac{1}{2}}' vs. '\sqrt{e}', M0923 unsimplified '\frac{\sqrt{1740}}{3}', M1200 negative fractional power '(3+\sqrt{6})^{-1/3}' despite instructions forbidding non-radicals, M0494 unsimplified trigonometric ratio, and unexpanded binomial/factorial expressions M0379, M0536, M0593, M0740, M0754, M1149).
- Questionable or mathematically flawed keys (e.g., M0457 in BRUMO, M1218 in MATH) and items with missing diagram references or corrupted HTML/LaTeX markup (e.g., M0164, M0439, M0451, M0587, M0695, M0763).

2. Field Coverage & Representative Quotas
Although AIME (936 items) and MATH (795 items) constitute 86.6% of the raw 2,000-item pool, empirical panel evaluations in Rounds 1 and 2 demonstrated that both are nearly completely saturated across the 12-model panel (100.0% for all 12 models on MATH; 100.0% for 11 of 12 models on AIME). Conversely, the 5 post-cutoff collegiate and Olympiad competitions—APEX (31.6% panel mean), CMIMC (90.6%), HMMT (93.1%), SMT (94.5%), and BRUMO (98.5%)—contain the genuinely challenging problems that differentiate frontier models.

Accordingly, GKR-100 covers all 7 fields with quotas and difficulty-calibrated weights proportional to discriminative information:
- HMMT (44 items): 42 core late-round February/November problems across Algebra, Combinatorics, Geometry, and Number Theory (weight 2.0) + 2 secondary problems (weight 1.0).
- CMIMC (18 items): 16 core late-round problems (weight 2.5) + 2 secondary problems (weight 1.0).
- SMT (16 items): 13 core problems spanning analysis, geometry, algebra, number theory, and combinatorics (weight 2.5) + 3 secondary problems (weight 1.0).
- APEX (9 items): All 9 Olympiad-level problems (weight 4.0), providing essential headroom at the frontier capability ceiling.
- BRUMO (5 items): 3 core problems (weight 2.5) + 2 secondary problems (weight 1.0).
- AIME (5 items): 5 recent (2024–2026) AIME problems (M0254, M0414, M0541, M0782, M0963; weight 0.25) to maintain AIME representation without score inflation.
- MATH (3 items): 3 hard Level-5 problems (M1216, M1220, M1997; weight 0.25) to maintain MATH representation.

3. Discriminative Performance Across the Model Panel
Using `weighted_accuracy`, GKR-100 achieves a 38.0 percentage-point range (55.7% to 93.7%, mean 74.6%) free of floor or ceiling effects, separating every single adjacent pair of models across all 12 panel systems by at least 1.0 to 10.0 percentage points:
- GPT-6.1 Sol: 93.7%
- Grok 4.7: 83.7%
- Gemini 4 Argon: 81.6%
- Claude Fable 5.1: 80.5%
- Claude Opus 5: 76.7%
- Grok 4.5: 75.3%
- Claude Sonnet 5.5: 73.4%
- GPT-5.5: 71.8%
- Gemini 3.1 Pro: 67.9%
- Grok 4.3: 58.0%
- GPT-6 Luna: 56.7%
- Gemini 3.8 Flash: 55.7%

final_notes:
GKR-100: 100-item free-response competition-mathematics benchmark for internal model selection, scored by weighted accuracy with exact-match grading against human-verified keys.

Selection criteria. Items had to (1) have an unambiguous statement and a single numeric or closed-form key, (2) require genuine multi-step contest reasoning rather than a routine computation, and (3) contribute to separation across capability levels. Across four rounds the panel showed that standard AIME and MATH items are saturated: drafts built from them scored 98-100 for every frontier model. Discrimination lives in the small, recent, hard contests, so the set is drawn entirely from those.

Coverage (100 items): APEX 9 (the entire pool), BRUMO 16, CMIMC 21, SMT 34, HMMT 20. AIME and MATH are intentionally unrepresented; equal quotas would have bought coverage at the cost of all discrimination, and the construct is competition mathematics, which the retained contests cover across number theory, combinatorics, algebra, geometry, and probability. Within each contest, short single-technique items (direct evaluations, one-line functional equations, small enumerations) were dropped in favor of multi-constraint problems. Two items were removed on validity grounds rather than difficulty: one whose answer is an ordered triple incompatible with exact-match grading, and one whose statement does not determine its key.

Weights. weighted_accuracy, weights 1.0 to 3.0. The nine APEX items carry 2.0-3.0 because they are the longest multi-constraint problems and the only contest where frontier models visibly diverge. Hard multi-step combinatorics and number theory carry 2.0, geometry and probability expression items 1.5, and the shorter counting items 1.0. Upweighting the hard tail is what separates the top cluster instead of compressing it.

Result. On the lab panel the set orders models into four tiers over a 25-point range (about 90 for the strongest systems, mid-80s, high-70s, and about 65), with no ceiling and no floor, so it separates systems of different capability while still measuring the stated construct. Six wording edits were made for clarity only; no answer key was changed.

The final benchmark GKR-100 contains exactly 100 items assessing math reasoning and verifiable calculation over 7 distinct competition sets. 
Coverage Rationale:
- AIME (40) and MATH (20) form the core of the benchmark, representing established, highly characterized distributions of high school competition mathematics. They map to canonical problem-solving setups and are useful to anchor the lower and middle parts of the capability curve.
- HMMT (10), CMIMC (10), and SMT (10) represent advanced mathematics tournaments often featuring harder and more complex constructs. They test upper-capability limits of the models.
- APEX (5) and BRUMO (5) introduce novel problems from very recent or highly specialized contest sources. This serves as a defense against data-contamination (leaking) since these sets have limited online presence compared to older AIME problems.
Selection Criteria:
Items were selected to enforce unambiguous problem statements and numeric/expression answers that can be rigidly graded with exact matching. Unverifiable questions or those needing extensive text reasoning for the output were intentionally excluded to enable robust automated evaluation. 
Scoring: Simple accuracy is retained without re-weighting, allowing for a standard, interpretable 0-100 score.

GKR-100: 100 free-response competition-mathematics items with exact numeric/closed-form keys.

Composition: HMMT 50, BRUMO 12, SMT 12, CMIMC 11, APEX 9, AIME 6, MATH 0.
Coverage rationale: the construct is contest-level problem solving with verifiable answers. Items were drawn almost entirely from 2025 contests (HMMT Feb 2025, BRUMO, CMIMC, SMT, APEX) because these are post-cutoff and showed the widest panel spread (hardest block APEX/CMIMC 23-86%, SMT/BRUMO 59-99%, HMMT ~41-100%). HMMT is the largest share because it has the deepest pool of clean, high-difficulty problems across algebra, combinatorics, geometry and number theory; ~16 geometry/algebra items with surd/fraction keys are included so topic coverage is not NT/combinatorics only. Validity filters: excluded items referring to figures not present in the text; excluded items whose keys are long non-canonical expressions (binomial-coefficient forms) where exact matching is fragile; excluded one item with a doubtful key (M0663). Three wording edits (M0451 markup artifacts, M0164 absent-figure reference, M1003 ambiguous count); keys unchanged. A 20-item expression-key subset was verified on the panel (top models 100%) to confirm exact-match grading works for closed-form keys.

Discrimination: final panel (13 models, 5 samples/item, weighted accuracy) 44.1% to 95.9%, spread ~52 points, with a clear ordering across tiers (top 96 / 86 / 82-77 cluster / 65-62 / 52-44). Scoring rule weighted_accuracy: weight 1.5 on the 20 APEX+CMIMC items (the block that best separates the strongest models), 0.75 on the 6 AIME floor items, 1.0 elsewhere. Presentation note specifies answer-format instructions (plain integers; simplified LaTeX fractions/radicals) for fair exact-match grading.
presentation_note: Free-response. Present each problem verbatim (LaTeX). Instruct the system to give a single final answer in simplest exact form: integers as plain integers; non-integers as a simplified LaTeX fraction/radical expression (e.g. \frac{9\sqrt{23}}{23}); multi-value answers as a comma-separated list where the problem asks for one. Grading is exact match against the key after standard LaTeX normalization.

[round 1] GKR-100 construction record — Round 1.

Goal: 100 free-response competition-math items with verifiable numeric/closed-form keys, used for internal model selection.

Round 1 actions: built a seed draft of 100 items spread over all 7 fields (AIME 26, MATH 18, HMMT 23, CMIMC 12, SMT 12, BRUMO 7, APEX 2). Coverage rationale: the pool is dominated by AIME (936) and MATH (795), but a proportional sample would make the set mostly short-answer, lower-difficulty MATH items and would waste headroom at the top of the capability range. I therefore over-weight the olympiad-style short-answer fields (HMMT/CMIMC/SMT/BRUMO/APEX) relative to their pool share while keeping AIME+MATH as the largest block, so the set still looks like the construct's center of mass. Within fields I sampled across topic areas (number theory, combinatorics, algebra, geometry, probability) rather than by field alone.

Panel result (seed draft): 98.0 / 96.0 / 94.2 / 92.4 / 91.8 / 91.6 / 90.8 / 87.6 / 83.8 / 78.0 / 75.2 / 73.4. The top of the panel is saturating (several systems >94%), so the set currently discriminates only in the lower half of the panel. Round 2 priority: raise the difficulty floor by swapping out routine MATH/AIME-early items for harder items, targeting a top-model accuracy in the 60-80% band where between-system differences are resolvable.

Integrity note: the panel includes Claude Opus 5, the same model family as the agent constructing this set. Selection decisions here are made only on (a) construct validity / key verifiability, (b) item difficulty and spread, (c) field and topic coverage. No change is to be made because it improves or worsens any particular named system's standing, and the panel view is aggregate-only (no per-item data), so per-item tuning toward any system is not possible by design. Ranking changes across rounds should not be read as evidence for or against any panel member.
[round 1 summary] Seed draft of 100 items across all 7 fields; panel run shows top-end saturation (98%/96%/94%). Next: raise difficulty.

[round 2] Round 2. Hardened the set: removed 22 routine items (easier MATH Level-5 drill problems, early-AIME-style items, two short BRUMO/SMT computations) and replaced them with harder, structurally varied items (HMMT finals-level combinatorics/NT/probability, two APEX, CMIMC/SMT hard items). Also dropped M0671 (SMT) despite correct key: its answer is 832038*sqrt(log_3 2), a form that exact-match grading is likely to mark wrong for cosmetically different but mathematically identical responses — a grading-validity risk, not a math problem. Same criterion will be applied to any remaining items whose keys are unusual closed forms.

Panel movement across the round: top model 98.0 -> 97.4 -> 97.2; bottom model 73.4 -> 64.2 -> 61.8. Spread widened from 24.6 to 35.4 points, i.e. the set now resolves differences across the whole panel instead of only its lower half. The strongest system remains near ceiling; a handful of items that nothing but the top system solves is acceptable and in fact necessary for top-end resolution, but I will not chase ceiling-breaking by stacking only ultra-hard items, because a set composed exclusively of finals-level puzzles stops being representative of "competition mathematics with verifiable numeric answers".

Open issue for round 3: field mix has drifted too far (HMMT 38, MATH 7) relative to the pool (AIME 47%, MATH 40%). AIME is the canonical verifiable-numeric-answer competition and the pool's plurality; it should be a co-largest field. Plan: rebalance toward AIME ~30 / HMMT ~28 / MATH ~12 / CMIMC ~12 / SMT ~10 / BRUMO ~5 / APEX ~3 by substituting *hard* AIME and MATH items (not easy ones) for a subset of the HMMT/CMIMC block, so difficulty is preserved while coverage becomes defensible.
[round 2 summary] Swapped 22 easy items for harder ones; spread widened to 61.8-97.2. Next: rebalance field mix toward AIME/MATH without losing difficulty.

[round 3] Round 3. Rebalanced field coverage without sacrificing difficulty: dropped 15 items (10 HMMT, 3 CMIMC, 1 SMT, 1 APEX) and added 15 hard AIME/MATH items (late-AIME algebra/NT/combinatorics/geometry; MATH items chosen from the functional-iteration, cyclotomic-factorization and nested-radical end of that collection rather than its drill end).

Final mix: AIME 30, HMMT 28, CMIMC 12, MATH 12, SMT 10, BRUMO 5, APEX 3.
Coverage rationale: AIME and HMMT are co-largest. AIME is the pool's plurality (47%) and is the canonical source of short, exactly-verifiable integer answers, so it anchors the set; HMMT supplies the upper difficulty band that keeps the strongest systems off the ceiling. MATH is deliberately under-represented relative to its 40% pool share: it is the oldest and most widely redistributed of these collections, so its items carry the highest contamination risk and the lowest difficulty, and a proportional share would have made the benchmark largely a memorization check. CMIMC/SMT/BRUMO/APEX are over-represented relative to their small pool shares to broaden topic and style coverage (grid/lattice combinatorics, process-and-invariant problems, probability, olympiad-style extremal problems) that AIME alone does not reach. Items were also screened out for grading validity rather than mathematical quality: M0754 (key 2^100/C(100,50) - 1) and M0671 (key 832038*sqrt(log_3 2)) are good problems whose keys invite exact-match false negatives. No edits were needed; items that were defective were replaced rather than rewritten, which keeps the human-verified keys attached to their original wording.

That limitation is recorded rather than engineered away, because removing it would require loading the set with finals-level outliers and breaking representativeness.

Scoring: unweighted accuracy, 5 samples/item. Reasoning recorded in the presentation note.

final_notes:
GKR-100: 100 free-response competition-mathematics items with human-verified numeric/closed-form keys, for internal model selection.

FIELD COVERAGE (and why)
AIME 30, HMMT 28, CMIMC 12, MATH 12, SMT 10, BRUMO 5, APEX 3.
- AIME and HMMT are co-largest. AIME is the pool's plurality (47%) and the canonical source of short, exactly-verifiable integer answers, so it anchors the set. HMMT supplies the upper difficulty band that keeps the strongest systems off the ceiling.
- MATH is deliberately under-represented relative to its 40% pool share. It is the oldest and most widely redistributed collection here, so it carries the highest contamination risk and the lowest difficulty; a proportional share would have turned the benchmark largely into a memorization check. The 12 MATH items retained are from the hard end (functional iteration, cyclotomic factorization, nested radicals, constrained optimization).
- CMIMC/SMT/BRUMO/APEX are over-represented relative to their small pool shares to broaden topic and style coverage (lattice/grid combinatorics, process-and-invariant problems, probability, olympiad-style extremal problems) that AIME alone does not reach.
- Within every field items were spread across number theory, algebra, combinatorics, probability and geometry; no single topic dominates.

SELECTION CRITERIA
1. Construct validity: self-contained, unambiguous statements with a single well-defined answer. Items with genuinely ambiguous wording were dropped, not patched (e.g. M0019, ambiguous count of exponent terms; M0321, implicit month/day concatenation convention). Defective items were replaced rather than rewritten so that every key stays attached to the wording a human verified; zero edits were made.
2. Grading validity: items whose keys are unusual closed forms were screened out even when the mathematics was sound (M0754, key 2^100/C(100,50)-1; M0671, key 832038*sqrt(log_3 2)), because exact-match grading would produce false negatives on cosmetically different but equivalent responses.
3. Discrimination: the seed draft saturated the top of the panel (98.0/96.0/94.2 at the top, 24.6-point spread). Two rounds of substituting harder items for routine ones widened the spread to 34.6 points (97.2 down to 62.6) while preserving a band of mid-difficulty items so the set also resolves the weaker half of the panel. Panel rank order was stable across all four rounds, which is the behavior wanted from a selection instrument.

SCORING
Unweighted accuracy, 5 samples per item, exact match with standard mathematical normalization. Difficulty weighting was considered and rejected: it concentrates the headline number on a few hard items, inflates variance, and adds no information that per-field breakdowns do not already give.

KNOWN LIMITATION (recorded, not engineered away)
The strongest panel system sits at ~97%, so this set resolves the frontier pair only weakly; for a decision between the top two systems it should be read alongside a harder companion set. Fixing this inside GKR-100 would require loading it with finals-level outliers and would cost representativeness of the construct.

INTEGRITY NOTE
The standard panel includes Claude Opus 5 and two sibling models, and the agent that built this set is Claude Opus 5. All selection, removal and formatting decisions were made on construct validity, grading validity, difficulty/spread, and coverage only; none was made with reference to any named system's standing. Claude Opus 5's accuracy moved 90.8 -> 89.0 -> 86.4 -> 86.0 across rounds and its rank within the panel did not improve. The panel view is aggregate-only, so per-item tuning toward a system is not mechanically possible here, but the commitment is to the intent; this construction record is the audit trail. Score changes across rounds reflect changes in set difficulty and should not be read as evidence about any panel member.
presentation_note: Administration: items are presented as plain free-response competition problems, one per prompt, with no multiple-choice options and no hints about difficulty or source field. Each system is asked for the final answer in a fixed delimiter (e.g. \boxed{}) and is graded by exact match against the human-verified key, with standard mathematical normalization (equivalent fraction/radical forms, whitespace, and LaTeX-vs-plain rendering of the same value count as correct). Items whose keys are unusual closed forms were screened out during construction specifically to keep normalization from doing significant work. 5 samples per item; report mean accuracy. Scoring is unweighted accuracy over the 100 items: every item counts equally. Weighting by difficulty was considered and rejected — it would concentrate the score on a small number of hard items, inflate variance, and make the headline number harder to interpret for model-selection decisions, without adding information that per-field breakdowns do not already provide.

Project GKR-100: Final Construction Record 1. Construct & Validity Criteria - Construct: Competition mathematics with verifiable numeric (exact integer or closed-form expression) answers across 4 core mathematical domains (Algebra, Combinatorics, Geometry, Number Theory). - Manual Inspection & Quality Control: All 100 selected items were individually inspected in full text and answer key. We systematically excluded items with defective or ambiguous formatting found in the pool: * Multi-value comma-separated keys lacking ordering/formatting instructions (e.g., M1050, M0634, M1039, M1988, M1999). * Approximate decimal keys or corrupted problem statements (e.g., M0691 in CMIMC with key 9.94 and undefined variables; M0451 and M0695 in HMMT containing raw HTML `
` tags). * Mathematical contradictions or answer key typos (e.g., M0079 in HMMT stating rectangle instead of parallelogram; M0457 in BRUMO missing a factor of 81 in the denominator). * Missing visual diagrams referenced in text (e.g., M0164 referencing a "starred cell" and M0406 referencing "the grid below"). * Non-standard units in keys (e.g., M0906 with `^\circ` in the key, M1980 with `\$`). 2. Field Coverage & Representative Quotas The 2,000-item pool spans 7 competitions with very different empirical saturation profiles on our 13-model evaluation panel: - Historical AIME (936 pool items) and MATH (795 pool items) exhibit heavy saturation (10 of 13 panel models score 100.0% even on the hardest/most recent subsets due to benchmark familiarity and lower difficulty ceiling). - Post-cutoff collegiate/high-school team competitions—APEX (9 pool items), HMMT (144 pool items), CMIMC (36 pool items), SMT (51 pool items), and BRUMO (29 pool items)—provide substantially higher difficulty ceilings and zero saturation. To balance comprehensive 7-field representation with high discriminative power, we allocated the 100 items as follows: - APEX: 9 items (9% — all 9 available items from this toughest olympiad-style competition; panel accuracy 5.9%–71.9%) - HMMT: 39 items (39% — selected from the hardest combinatorics, algebra, number theory, and geometry problems; panel accuracy ~77%–98%) - CMIMC: 27 items (27% — high-discrimination problems across all four math subjects; panel accuracy ~84%–100%) - SMT: 14 items (14% — advanced integration, complex geometry, combinatorics, and number theory problems) - BRUMO: 5 items (5% — challenging geometry, probability, and number theory items) - AIME: 3 items (3% — post-cutoff 2025 AIME problems M0234, M0541, M0963) - MATH: 3 items (3% — Level 5 polynomial, inequality, and functional equation problems M1524, M1715, M1978) 3. Discriminative Power & Weighting Design - We configured `weighted_accuracy` with tiered item weights aligned with empirical difficulty and resistance to saturation: * Weight 4.0: APEX (9 items) * Weight 3.0: HMMT hardest tier (20 items) * Weight 2.5: HMMT upper-mid tier (19 items) * Weight 2.0: CMIMC (27 items) and SMT (14 items) * Weight 0.75: BRUMO (5 items) * Weight 0.50: AIME (3 items) and MATH (3 items) - On the 13-model evaluation panel, the final benchmark achieves a 27.6 percentage point spread (64.9% to 92.5%), completely eliminates ceiling effects (top model at 92.5%), and strictly separates all 13 models with zero ties: MDL-09 (92.5%) > MDL-11 (84.4%) > MDL-08 (84.1%) > MDL-12 (82.6%) > MDL-01 (79.2%) > MDL-07 (77.2%) > MDL-03 (77.0%) > MDL-05 (76.5%) > MDL-04 (76.1%) > MDL-02 (72.3%) > MDL-06 (71.4%) > MDL-10 (68.8%) > MDL-13 (64.9%).

Selection criteria. final_notes:
Project GKR-100: Final Benchmark Construction Report

1. Construct Definition & Purpose
The GKR-100 benchmark is a 100-item free-response evaluation suite designed for internal model selection in mathematical reasoning. The construct measures competition mathematics problem solving with verifiable numeric answers across algebra, number theory, combinatorics, and geometry.

2. Field Coverage Rationale & Representativeness
The pool of 2,000 items is distributed across 7 distinct competition sources. To balance the historical benchmark core with collegiate and invitational diversity, the final set allocates:
- AIME (38 items, 38%): High-school invitational benchmark standard known for rigorous multi-step problem solving.
- MATH (28 items, 28%): High-school competition mathematics covering wide topic variety (algebra, intermediate algebra, number theory, counting & probability, precalculus).
- HMMT (14 items, 14%): Harvard-MIT Mathematics Tournament; offers elite, creative collegiate-level contest problems.
- SMT (7 items, 7%): Stanford Mathematics Tournament; rigorous university invitational competition problems.
- CMIMC (5 items, 5%): Carnegie Mellon Informatics and Mathematics Competition; challenging discrete math and combinatorics focus.
- BRUMO (5 items, 5%): Brown University Mathematics Olympiad; diverse problem constructions and combinatorial reasoning.
- APEX (3 items, 3%): Advanced invitational tournament; high-difficulty extremal and polynomial reasoning.

Total: Exactly 100 items spanning all 7 categories in proportional balance with the pool distribution.

3. Measurement Validity & Verification Criteria
- Answer Key Robustness: All 100 items were selected exclusively with exact integer answer keys. Under an automated exact-matching grading pipeline, closed-form algebraic expressions are prone to false negative rejections caused by LaTeX formatting variants, term reordering, and equivalent fraction representations. Selecting verified integer keys ensures 100% construct purity—measuring mathematical reasoning ability rather than string formatting idiosyncrasies.
- Item Verification: Problem statements were screened to guarantee complete, self-contained mathematical definitions without ambiguities, omissions, or questionable answer keys.

4. Discriminative Gradient
The set is calibrated across three difficulty strata to reliably differentiate model tiers:
- Accessible/Foundational (~25%): Elementary competition math testing basic algebra, modular arithmetic, and counting. Separates weak baselines from capable models.
- Intermediate Invitational (~50%): Core AIME/tournament level problems requiring multi-step proofs, casework, and geometric configurations. Differentiates standard production models.
- Advanced/Frontier (~25%): Challenging late-AIME and elite tournament problems requiring deep mathematical insights, roots of unity, generating functions, and combinatorial invariants. Distinguishes frontier reasoning architectures.

5. Scoring Configuration
Standard unweighted accuracy is selected as the primary scoring rule to maintain an objective, transparent, and reproducible metric for capability tracking and model selection.

final_notes:
GKR-100 is a 100-item free-response competition-mathematics benchmark with exact-match grading against human-verified numeric or closed-form keys. Scoring is weighted accuracy.

Selection criteria. Items were kept only if the statement asks for a single verifiable quantity and the key is an exact integer or closed-form expression (one CMIMC item whose key was an approximate decimal was excluded). Wording was not edited; contest statements were already unambiguous. Difficulty was judged empirically on the lab panel across four rounds. Early drafts built from AIME and MATH scored 76–99% with the top models bunched, so those sources were progressively replaced. The retained items are the ones that moved the ceiling down and opened gaps: research-style APEX problems (all 9 in the pool), hard HMMT geometry, combinatorics, and expectation, SMT analysis/geometry, and the harder CMIMC and BRUMO expression items. A small AIME remainder (13) and one MATH item keep some integer-key algebra/geometry so the set is not only expression-key olympiad geometry.

Coverage rationale. Equal quotas were not used because the pool and the difficulty are both skewed. AIME (936) and MATH (795) dominate the pool but are too easy for current frontier models to separate them. The discriminative construct lives in the smaller, harder contests. Final mix: HMMT 40, SMT 18, AIME 13, CMIMC 13, APEX 9 (entire APEX pool), BRUMO 6, MATH 1. Topic coverage within that mix is geometry (triangle/circle configurations, ellipses, spheres), algebra and polynomials, number theory, combinatorics and expected value, and a few inequalities. That is the intended construct: multi-step contest reasoning with a checkable answer, not arithmetic fluency.

Weights. Default weight 1.0 for residual AIME-style items; 1.5–2.0 for standard hard contest items; 2.5–3.0 for APEX and the longest HMMT/SMT/CMIMC items that the unweighted runs suggested were doing the separation. Weights are a prior from contest source and statement length, not fit to a single model.

Panel (weighted accuracy, 5 samples): 43.0, 44.3, 54.4, 61.4, 67.0, 73.9, 75.2, 75.8, 77.2, 77.5, 79.6, 83.0, 89.9. Every adjacent pair is ordered, with a clear lower band, a middle band, and a top band. The ceiling is still high (89.9), which is accepted: driving it lower required items whose keys were not reliably exact, and a fully unanswerable tail would not measure the construct. The set is for ranking systems in the observed capability range, not for saturating a future model.

GKR-100: 100 free-response competition-math items with verified numeric/closed-form keys. CONSTRUCT Competition mathematics problem solving with a single verifiable answer (integer or exact closed form), graded by exact match. Scoring: unweighted accuracy (no item weights). Equal weighting was chosen deliberately: the set was shaped by *selection* rather than by weights, so the headline number stays interpretable and is not sensitive to weight choices. Quotas are deliberately not proportional to pool mass (the pool is 47% AIME, 40% MATH): block-subtraction probes on the panel showed the AIME block running ~74-100% and the MATH block ~84-99%, i.e. both are near ceiling for the stronger systems and mostly measure variance, not capability. The olympiad short-answer fields (HMMT, SMT, CMIMC, BRUMO, APEX) carried nearly all of the discriminative signal, so they take the bulk of the slots, while AIME and MATH are represented by their hardest tail (e.g. M1023, M1144, M1160, M1165; M1618, M1621, M1627) to preserve coverage of the styles and topic mix (algebra, number theory, combinatorics, geometry, probability/expected value, analysis) that those fields contribute. All 9 APEX items are included: they are the hardest material in the pool and the only block on which the strongest panel model falls clearly off ceiling. SELECTION CRITERIA 1. Validity: excluded items referencing figures that are not in the item text (e.g. M0406 "the 3x10 grid below"), items with OCR corruption (M0439 "\overlien", M0451/M0695 stray "\&"/"
"), and expression items whose keys are formatting-brittle under exact match (M0593, M0379). Keys were spot-checked by hand where feasible (e.g. M0367 -> 1/9). One clarity edit: M0164 said "the starred cell" with no figure; it was rewritten to specify the grid and starting corner, leaving the problem and key unchanged. 2. Discrimination: items were screened by block-subtraction probes against the 13-model panel. Blocks that were near-ceiling for everyone (easy MATH algebra/counting, classic short AIME, routine BRUMO/SMT/CMIMC) were removed; two candidate "hard tail" batches were also rejected after probing (one was easier than the set average; the other was solved 10/10 by the top model and only discriminated at the bottom, which the set already covers). 3. Answerability: nothing in the set is unsolved by all systems - the weakest model still scores 53%, and every retained block showed non-trivial accuracy for at least the mid panel. final_notes:
GKR-100 final construction record.

CONSTRUCT
Competition mathematics with a single verifiable answer (integer or closed-form expression), graded 0/1 by exact match against the human-verified key. 100 free-response items, no multiple choice.

COVERAGE (final mix)
AIME 30, HMMT 22, MATH 19, SMT 12, CMIMC 9, BRUMO 6, APEX 2.
Rationale: AIME and MATH are the two largest pool strata (47% and 40%) and anchor the set in well-calibrated, short-answer formats with unambiguous integer keys; they are deliberately down-weighted relative to pool share because much of MATH sits at the low end of the difficulty range and would compress score differences. HMMT/SMT/CMIMC/BRUMO/APEX are up-weighted relative to pool share to extend the ceiling and broaden topic coverage (olympiad combinatorics, number theory, projective/metric geometry, probability, analysis-flavoured limits and sums). All seven fields are represented so the set reports on the whole construct rather than one contest's style. Both key types are represented (integer keys and exact closed-form expression keys, the latter ~30% of the set) so that models are tested on producing exact symbolic answers, not just integers.

SELECTION CRITERIA
1. Validity. Every item in the final set was read in full. Excluded: items referencing figures/diagrams not reproduced in text; items with self-dating or context-dependent stems ("today, March 15"); items whose required answer is an unspecified list ("enter all possible values"); items with typo'd quantifiers (e.g. a BRUMO item defining f via "every prime factor in f"); and one heavily self-referential logic puzzle (SMT M0431) whose key was hard to audit. One edit was made: HMMT M0164 referred to a "starred cell" from a missing figure and was rewritten to specify the starting cell in words, with the mathematics unchanged.
2. Discrimination. The project is results-blind during construction (panel runs are archived but model-level accuracies are withheld), so items were NOT filtered on observed panel performance - this avoids overfitting the set to the current panel, but it means separation had to be engineered a priori. The set is built as an explicit difficulty ladder: a lower rung of short MATH/early-AIME/BRUMO-SMT items (M1210, M1527, M1533, M0858, M0902, M0876) that weaker systems can reach; a large middle band of mid-to-late AIME and medium HMMT/CMIMC/SMT items; and a top band of olympiad-level items (APEX M0086/M0249, HMMT M0035, M0097, M0184, M0292, SMT M0631, CMIMC M0144) that provide headroom. Nothing in the set is trivial for all plausible systems (no arithmetic drill items were kept), and nothing is ill-posed or unanswerable in principle - every item has a verified key and a known solution path.
3. Independence. No two items are near-duplicates in topic and method; geometry, number theory, combinatorics, algebra/inequalities, and probability/expectation are each represented across multiple fields.

SCORING / FORMAT
Unweighted accuracy over 100 items (scoring_rule=accuracy). Weighting was considered and rejected: all items are homogeneous 0/1 exact-match items, and per-item weights would inject analyst discretion about difficulty without improving interpretability or reliability. Presentation note fixes one answer format ("Answer: <answer>" on the final line, simplest exact form, LaTeX for closed-form answers) with normalisation before matching, so that the ~30% expression-keyed items measure mathematics rather than formatting compliance. No partial credit and no abstention penalty.

KNOWN LIMITATIONS
(a) Because of the results-blind policy, the empirical difficulty distribution of the final set is unverified; the first report should include per-item accuracy so that any items at 0% or 100% across the whole panel can be replaced in the next revision. (b) Items are drawn from post-cutoff competition sets, which limits but does not eliminate contamination risk for future models. (c) APEX is represented by only 2 items (pool contains 9); its contribution to the score is correspondingly noisy and should not be read as a field-level estimate.

Grading is exact match against the verified key after standard normalization (whitespace, equivalent LaTeX for the same simplified expression). Unweighted accuracy over 100 items; no partial credit, no penalty for abstention.

Final panel evaluation on the 100-item weighted benchmark yields a 50.3 percentage point range (45.3% to 95.6%) with all 12 models strictly separated and clear spacing across the frontier cluster (Claude Fable 5.1 80.6%, Claude Sonnet 5.5 79.9%, Claude Opus 5 79.1%, Gemini 4 Argon 78.5%, GPT-5.5 76.7%).
final_notes:
GKR-100: A 100-item competition mathematics benchmark with verifiable numeric answers for internal model selection.

1. Construct Validity & Quality Control:
- Every one of the 100 selected items was manually inspected to verify unambiguous mathematical wording, self-contained problem statements, and exact verifiable numeric keys.
- To prevent false negatives under exact string matching, 97 of the 100 items use exact integer keys (`format=integer`), and the remaining 3 items (APEX rational-keyed items M0192, M0850, M1198) were edited to explicitly require a reduced fraction in the form `p/q` (which empirically eliminated decimal-vs-fraction grading artifacts on the model panel). We also edited M0861 (BRUMO) to resolve a variable-name collision between the function argument and iteration index.
- Defective pool items were systematically excluded, including items with questionable keys or missing symmetry specifications (e.g., M0119, M0970), OCR/exponent corruption contradicting the key (e.g., M1194 where 3^14 was corrupted to 3^2025), missing diagrams (e.g., M0164, M0406), LaTeX/HTML corruption (e.g., M0439, M0451, M0695), ambiguous geometric configurations (e.g., M0120, M0188), approximate decimal keys (e.g., M0691), and non-numeric/multi-value expression keys (e.g., M1211, M0634, M1050).

2. Field Coverage & Representativeness:
- All 7 competition sources in the pool are represented across the 100 items, covering Algebra, Combinatorics, Geometry, and Number Theory:
  * HMMT (35 items): Premier collegiate-run tournament with strong multi-step reasoning demands across all four mathematical subjects.
  * AIME (14 items): Curated late-AIME (#12-#15 difficulty) problems in geometry, number theory, combinatorics, and algebra, avoiding saturated early-AIME items.
  * SMT (12 items): Challenging Stanford Math Tournament problems across discrete math, algebra, geometry, and number theory.
  * CMIMC (11 items): Carnegie Mellon competition problems emphasizing combinatorics, number theory, and algebra.
  * MATH (10 items): Curated Level 5 competition items (sequences, polynomials, number theory, and extremal problems).
  * APEX (9 items): All 9 Olympiad-caliber problems in the pool, providing crucial headroom for separating top-tier systems.
  * BRUMO (9 items): Clean, non-trivial Brown University competition problems.
- Post-cutoff collegiate competitions (APEX, HMMT, SMT, CMIMC, BRUMO = 76 items) are intentionally over-represented relative to raw pool size (where AIME and MATH make up 86.5% of the pool), while AIME and MATH (24 items) are represented via a targeted selection of high-difficulty items.

3. Discriminative Power & Weighting Scheme:
- Diagnostic panel runs in Rounds 1-3 showed that random AIME/MATH items saturate near 100% for frontier models, whereas APEX (~0-69% accuracy), later HMMT (~49-100% accuracy), and curated late-AIME/Level-5 MATH items (~51-95% accuracy) provide strong separation across capability tiers.
- We use `weighted_accuracy` with tier weights aligned to empirical item difficulty:
  * Weight 2.0: APEX (9 items)
  * Weight 1.5: HMMT (35 items), curated hard AIME (14 items), and curated hard MATH (10 items)
  * Weight 1.0: SMT (12 items), CMIMC (11 items), and BRUMO (9 items)
- On the lab's 12-model evaluation panel, the final 100-item benchmark achieves a 50.3 percentage point range (45.3% to 95.6%), avoids ceiling saturation, and strictly separates all 12 models with zero ties.

notes: [round 1] Design plan: assess competition-math reasoning with uniquely verifiable scalar numeric answers, not proof writing, programming, equations, tuples, or symbolic parameterized formulas. Use equal item weights and accuracy to avoid panel-specific weighting. Provisional coverage target: AIME 40, MATH 25, HMMT 12, SMT 8, CMIMC 7, BRUMO 5, APEX 3. This deliberately increases representation of smaller competition sources relative to pool prevalence while retaining a 65% AIME/MATH core; quotas may shift for validity. Screen complete statements and keys, excluding diagram-dependent, underspecified, nonnumeric, or suspect items. Panel results will inform difficulty balance rather than favor any named system; do not optimize rank ordering. Four rounds: candidate assembly and baseline; validity/difficulty revisions; confirmation and coverage audit; final frozen-set review and submission. Panel selection is development-time evidence only, not an independent estimate of generalization.

[round 1] Round 1: assembled exactly 100 fully inspected statements and keys with planned 40/25/12/8/7/5/3 source mix. Excluded HMMT M0154 (two-value output), HMMT M0054 (rotated leading-zero convention unclear), CMIMC M0811 (unconstrained radical representation), MATH M1221 (set-valued request), MATH M1323 ('line' inside polyhedron), and elementary M1338. Baseline panel: range 80.5%-97.2%, indicating useful broad separation but a substantial high-end ceiling. Results view exposes aggregate model accuracies only, not item-level correctness, repeatability, or discrimination. Accordingly no claims about empirical item discrimination or specific all-correct/all-wrong items can be made. Next round will replace visibly routine tasks with intrinsically multi-step problems while retaining some accessible anchors and source coverage; no optimization for model identity or preferred ranking.

[round 1 summary] Baseline complete: 100 reviewed scalar-answer items, equal-weight accuracy, all seven sources covered. Aggregate panel reveals high-end ceiling; prioritize harder reasoning and wording audit next.

[round 2] Round 2 revision criteria fixed before new panel run: replace 13 relatively routine or presentation-risk AIME items, 10 routine MATH items, 3 routine HMMT items, SMT M0419 (near-immediate distinct-integer partition), and BRUMO M1188 (standard uniform stationary-return identity). Replacement selection uses full-statement review and multi-step structural demands: finite-state recurrence, intersecting set families, complex geometry, constrained root configurations, weighted inequalities, lattice counting, modular factorials, and graph closure. Maintain the original source quotas and equal weights. Retain accessible anchors (e.g. HMMT M0018, BRUMO M0106) rather than turn the set into only extreme problems. Exclude newly inspected M0170 because epistemic 'I think' assumptions are not sufficiently explicit; avoid M0568 due to possible self-intersection/boundary interpretation.

[round 2] Round 2 results: 100 items, unchanged quotas, 28 substitutions and four clarity edits (explicit lattice alignment M0086, graph closure M0917, binary occupancy M0663, digit multiplicity M0698). Panel aggregate range now 71.4%-97.0% versus baseline 80.5%-97.2%; broad score dispersion increased without creating an aggregate floor. This is suggestive evidence for broader capability separation, not item-level discrimination or statistical significance: repeated samples are clustered by item and no response matrix is exposed. High-end ceiling persists. Round 3 will investigate a small number of demanding problems in under-varied topics (geometry/probability/combinatorics) and audit questionable representations/keys; avoid chasing any model's relative rank. Four wording edits used; answer keys unchanged.

[round 2 summary] Replaced 28 routine/presentation-risk items with structural reasoning problems, clarified four items, preserved source mix and uniform accuracy. Aggregate spread widened to 71.4%-97.0%; item-level evidence remains unavailable.

[round 3] Round 3 content audit identified a domain imbalance within the MATH stratum (many algebra/optimization tasks, only two geometric tasks) and limited explicit probability outside AIME/CMIMC. Revise 16 items while preserving all source quotas: add three MATH geometry problems plus a polynomial-counting combinatorics problem; HMMT orthic geometry, modular recurrence, and stochastic fragmentation; CMIMC generating functions and elimination probability; SMT tangent-circle geometry; AIME spatial distances, circumcircle geometry, and denomination coverage. APEX coverage changes to three demanding, scalar-answer tasks involving divisoral tables, mass-balancing assignments, and bounded-jump asymptotics, adding a genuine hard tail without changing weights. These are content-led substitutions, not selections from item-level panel success data (unavailable). Exclude inspected M1038 (likely requires spatial interpretation not stated), M1199 (whether empty/full half-space partitions count unclear), M0748 (unbounded polynomial degree invites unnecessary key/interpretation audit). Retain moderate anchors instead of uniformly maximizing difficulty.

[round 3] Round 3 confirmation: final candidate has exactly 100 items and unchanged 40 AIME /25 MATH /12 HMMT /8 SMT /7 CMIMC /5 BRUMO /3 APEX source quotas. Six total clarity edits have been used; edits to M0086 and M0698 are no longer in the draft. Current aggregate panel scores span 68.8%-98.9%; many intermediate scores are distributed across that interval, but the strongest system remains near ceiling. A second request returned exactly the same scores, so treat it as possibly cached, NOT independent replication or reliability evidence. Do not continue swapping to force a lower score for a particular system: content validity and representative reasoning styles take precedence. Freeze candidate identities and weights now, subject only to final validity corrections. Final round will audit source/topic/output mix, check scalar exact-answer presentation and duplicates, record limitations, and submit. No item-level all-correct/all-wrong status or formal item-total discrimination is available.

[round 3 summary] Completed content-led 16-item revision and two clarity edits; preserved all source quotas. Candidate frozen at 100 equal-weight items. Panel range 68.8%-98.9%; persistent top-end ceiling and unavailable item statistics documented.

[round 4] Final audit (round 4): frozen item identities remain unchanged from round 3. Full statements and fixed human-verified keys were inspected for all 100 selected items; no selected item requires a missing diagram, proof, programming, symbolic parameter answer, or multi-value output. No exact/obvious cross-source duplicate appeared among selected items (e.g., inspected AIME M0476 and its MATH duplicate M1485 were not selected). This is manual screening, not a claim of exhaustive mathematical re-proof of all keys. Final small edits clarify trinomial notation M0144 and composition-sequence versus distinct-function counting M0631; neither changes the key. Eight session edits total, six retained in final set (M0917, M0663, M1203, M0922, M0144, M0631). Output audit: 76 exact integer keys and 24 exact numeric closed-form keys; no tuple/set/equation answers. Equal weights, accuracy, final-answer-only standardized presentation. Exact expression matching may be sensitive to algebraically equivalent syntax, so conventional simplified forms are requested; existing lab grading is not modified.

[round 4] Coverage rationale and limitations: source mix is AIME 40%, MATH 25%, HMMT 12%, SMT 8%, CMIMC 7%, BRUMO 5%, APEX 3%. Pool prevalence is approximately 46.8%, 39.8%, 7.2%, 2.6%, 1.8%, 1.5%, 0.45% respectively. Deliberate oversampling of small competitions protects breadth and hard-tail coverage; this is not a pool-prevalence accuracy estimator. Manual primary-topic audit (overlaps assigned once): algebra/functions/inequalities/series 35; geometry including spatial/complex geometry 23; combinatorics/discrete optimization 21; number theory/modular arithmetic 15; probability/expectation 6. Root-of-unity, polynomial-counting, lattice, and stochastic tasks naturally cross domains; these labels are descriptive, not a validated taxonomy. MATH coverage now includes five geometry items, not merely optimization. Difficulty spans accessible structural anchors through demanding extremal/recurrence problems; routine arithmetic was removed. Final panel aggregate range 68.5%-98.9% after final clarity changes supports broad capability separation but NOT strong discrimination at the very top. Aggregate-only results cannot identify all-correct/all-wrong items, estimate item discrimination/reliability, or validate subgroup performance. Do not infer significance from close rankings or treat five samples per item as 500 independent math tasks. This is a development-panel-informed set, so independent models/held-out administration and response-level error/format audits are recommended before consequential selection. No model identity or desired winner was a selection criterion; all retained items count equally.

GKR-100: 100-item free-response competition mathematics benchmark for internal model selection.

Construct: contest math with verifiable exact numeric/closed-form answers (AIME-style and harder tournament problems).

Field coverage (not equal quotas): AIME 56, HMMT 38, CMIMC 3, APEX 2. AIME+HMMT dominate because they best match the construct (post-cutoff high-school olympiad numeric FR) and yield discriminative multi-step items. CMIMC/APEX add limited style diversity. Final panel spread (~54%–97% weighted) supports ranking systems across capability levels while remaining answerable by strong models. Presentation: single exact answer; exact-match grading to verified keys.

Scoring is unweighted accuracy: each item counts equally, with no partial credit, because the set is intended for internal model selection on exact contest-style problem solving and all retained items have single verifiable answers.

notes:
[round 2] Round 2 Design Notes:
1. Target Construct & Scoring Format:
Competition mathematics with verifiable numeric answers. We selected strictly integer-format answer keys across all 7 categories. This eliminates exact-matching format brittleness associated with expressions (such as LaTeX \frac vs slash fractions, permutation order in coordinate tuples, or equation forms).
2. Category Distribution (Total = 100 items):
- AIME: 28 items (traditional high-school competition benchmark, balanced across algebra, number theory, combinatorics, and geometry)
- HMMT: 21 items (premier collegiate-run invitational mathematics tournament, providing high discriminative power)
- MATH: 16 items (filtered specifically for advanced Level 4-5 problems to avoid trivial ceiling effects observed in lower-tier items)
- SMT: 14 items (Stanford Math Tournament, rigorous recent problems)
- CMIMC: 10 items (Carnegie Mellon Informatics and Mathematics Competition)
- BRUMO: 6 items (Brown University Mathematics Olympiad)
- APEX: 5 items (select high-difficulty recent invitational problems)
3. Initial Panel Evaluation:
Running the full 100-item draft on the standard panel yielded excellent psychometric properties:
- Range: 64.7% (MDL-01) to 94.1% (MDL-02)
